claim: The brain possesses a remarkable capacity to compensate for changes in inputs resulting from a range of sensory impairments.
source: The brain possesses a remarkable capacity to compensate for changes in inputs resulting from a range of sensory impairments.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge about neural plasticity and sensory compensation.

claim: Adaptation to asymmetric hearing loss can be achieved either by reinterpreting altered spatial cues or by relying more on those cues that remain intact.
source: Developmental studies of sound localization have shown that adaptation to asymmetric hearing loss can be achieved either by reinterpreting altered spatial cues or by relying more on those cues that remain intact.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to developmental studies, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Adaptation to monaural deprivation in adulthood is possible but appears to lack flexibility.
source: Adaptation to monaural deprivation in adulthood is also possible, but appears to lack such flexibility.
evidence: This statement reflects prior understanding in the field before the current study's findings.

claim: Appropriate behavioral training enables monaurally-deprived adult humans to exploit both adaptive processes (cue remapping and reweighting).
source: Here we show, however, that appropriate behavioral training enables monaurally-deprived adult humans to exploit both of these adaptive processes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cortical recordings in ferrets reared with asymmetric hearing loss suggest that cue remapping and reweighting have distinct neural substrates.
source: Moreover, cortical recordings in ferrets reared with asymmetric hearing loss suggest that these forms of plasticity have distinct neural substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by neurophysiological data from ferrets presented in the study.

claim: The ability to adapt to asymmetric hearing loss using multiple adaptive processes is shared by different species.
source: An ability to adapt to asymmetric hearing loss using multiple adaptive processes is therefore shared by different species and may persist throughout the lifespan.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of human and ferret data in the study.

claim: The ability to adapt to asymmetric hearing loss using multiple adaptive processes may persist throughout the lifespan.
source: An ability to adapt to asymmetric hearing loss using multiple adaptive processes is therefore shared by different species and may persist throughout the lifespan.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the finding that adults can use both adaptive processes.

claim: The statistical structure of sensory experience varies across different environments.
source: This is important because the statistical structure of sensory experience varies across different environments (Mlynarski and Jost, 2014; Qian et al., 2012; Seydell et al., 2010), but also because long-term changes in sensory input result from a range of sensory impairments (Feldman and Brecht, 2005; Keating and King, 2015; Sengpiel, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Long-term changes in sensory input result from a range of sensory impairments.
source: This is important because the statistical structure of sensory experience varies across different environments (Mlynarski and Jost, 2014; Qian et al., 2012; Seydell et al., 2010), but also because long-term changes in sensory input result from a range of sensory impairments (Feldman and Brecht, 2005; Keating and King, 2015; Sengpiel, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Adaptation to altered inputs has been demonstrated in different sensory systems, particularly during development.
source: Adaptation to altered inputs has been demonstrated in different sensory systems, particularly during development, and serves to shape neural circuits to the specific inputs experienced by the individual (Margolis et al., 2014; Mendonca, 2014; Schreiner and Polley, 2014; Sur et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Adaptation to altered inputs serves to shape neural circuits to the specific inputs experienced by the individual.
source: Adaptation to altered inputs has been demonstrated in different sensory systems, particularly during development, and serves to shape neural circuits to the specific inputs experienced by the individual (Margolis et al., 2014; Mendonca, 2014; Schreiner and Polley, 2014; Sur et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Many ecologically important aspects of neural processing require the integration of multiple sensory cues.
source: However, many ecologically important aspects of neural processing require the integration of multiple sensory cues, either within or across different sensory modalities (Seilheimer et al., 2014; Seydell et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Monaural deprivation alters the binaural spatial cues that normally determine the perceived location of a sound in the horizontal plane.
source: Monaural deprivation alters the binaural spatial cues that normally determine the perceived location of a sound in the horizontal plane (Figure 1A) (Kumpik et al., 2010; Lupo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Adaptation to monaural deprivation can be achieved by learning the altered relationships between particular cue values and spatial locations (cue remapping).
source: Adaptation can therefore be achieved by learning the altered relationships between particular cue values and spatial locations (Gold and Knudsen, 2000; Keating et al., 2015; Knudsen et al., 1984), a process referred to as cue remapping.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In mammals, monaural spectral cues are available to judge sound source location in both the horizontal and vertical planes.
source: However, at least in mammals, monaural spectral cues are also available to judge sound source location in both the horizontal and vertical planes (Carlile et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Monaural spectral cues arise from the acoustic properties of the head and external ears, which filter sounds in a direction-dependent way.
source: These spectral cues arise from the acoustic properties of the head and external ears, which filter sounds in a direction-dependent way (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Monaural deprivation has no effect on the spectral cues available to the non-deprived ear.
source: Monaural deprivation has no effect on the spectral cues available to the non-deprived ear.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of monaural deprivation affecting only one ear.

claim: Adaptation to monaural deprivation can occur by learning to rely more on unchanged spectral cues whilst learning to ignore altered binaural cues (cue reweighting).
source: This means it is possible to adapt by learning to rely more on these unchanged spectral cues, whilst learning to ignore the altered binaural cues (Kacelnik et al., 2006; Keating et al., 2013; Kumpik et al., 2010), a form of adaptation referred to as cue reweighting.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adult humans trained to localize sounds while wearing an earplug showed gradual improvement in sound localization performance across training sessions.
source: Across training sessions, sound localization performance (% correct) gradually improved (Figure 1C–F; slope values >0; bootstrap test, p<0.01; Cohen's d = 1.43), indicating that relatively short periods of training are sufficient to drive adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C-F and statistical analysis.

claim: Relatively short periods of training are sufficient to drive adaptation to monaural deprivation in adult humans.
source: Across training sessions, sound localization performance (% correct) gradually improved (Figure 1C–F; slope values >0; bootstrap test, p<0.01; Cohen's d = 1.43), indicating that relatively short periods of training are sufficient to drive adaptation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed improvement in performance with training.

claim: Less improvement in sound localization performance was observed for random-spectrum sounds than for flat-spectrum sounds.
source: Consequently, if subjects adapt to asymmetric hearing loss by giving greater weight to the spectral cues provided by the non-deprived ear, we would expect to see less improvement in sound localization performance for random-spectrum sounds than for flat-spectrum sounds. This is precisely what we found (Figure 1E,F; random-spectrum slope values < flat-spectrum slope values; bootstrap test, p<0.01; Cohen's d = 1.18; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that adaptation involves learning to rely more on spectral cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E-F and statistical analysis.

claim: Adaptation to monaural deprivation involves learning to rely more on spectral cues.
source: This is precisely what we found (Figure 1E,F; random-spectrum slope values < flat-spectrum slope values; bootstrap test, p<0.01; Cohen's d = 1.18; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that adaptation involves learning to rely more on spectral cues.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential improvement for flat vs. random spectrum sounds.

claim: Spectral cues require a comparison of sound energy at different frequencies, which is not possible for narrowband sounds such as pure tones.
source: This is because spectral cues require a comparison of sound energy at different frequencies, which is not possible for these sounds (Figure 1B) (Carlile et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Improved localization of pure tones indicates adaptive processing of binaural cues.
source: Improved localization of pure tones would therefore indicate adaptive processing of binaural cues.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of cues available for pure tone localization.

claim: Interaural time differences (ITDs) are the primary cues for localizing low-frequency tones (<1.5 kHz).
source: Because interaural time differences (ITDs) and interaural level differences (ILDs) are respectively the primary cues for localizing low- (<1.5 kHz) and high-frequency (≥1.5 kHz) tones (Blauert, 1997), we tested each of these stimuli separately.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Interaural level differences (ILDs) are the primary cues for localizing high-frequency tones (≥1.5 kHz).
source: Because interaural time differences (ITDs) and interaural level differences (ILDs) are respectively the primary cues for localizing low- (<1.5 kHz) and high-frequency (≥1.5 kHz) tones (Blauert, 1997), we tested each of these stimuli separately.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Subjects showed improvements in their ability to localize both low- and high-frequency pure tones over time, demonstrated by a decline in error magnitude.
source: We observed improvements in subjects' ability to localize both low- and high-frequency pure tones over time, demonstrated by a decline in error magnitude (Figure 2E,F; Δ error <0; bootstrap test, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2E-F and statistical analysis.

claim: The initial bias toward the side of the open ear was reduced with training.
source: The initial bias toward the side of the open ear was also reduced (Figure 2G,H; Δ bias <0; bootstrap test, p<0.01; low-frequency, Cohen's d = 0.7; high-frequency, Cohen's d = 0.96).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2G-H and statistical analysis.

claim: Adaptation to monaural deprivation involves a shift in the mapping of altered binaural cues onto spatial location.
source: Adaptation therefore involves a shift in the mapping of altered binaural cues onto spatial location.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed reduction in bias and error magnitude for pure tones.

claim: Subjects adapted to monaural deprivation using a combination of both cue remapping and cue reweighting.
source: Together, these results show that subjects adapted to monaural deprivation using a combination of both cue remapping and cue reweighting.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the experimental findings showing both types of adaptation.

claim: Cue remapping and cue reweighting share a similar time-course.
source: Although cue remapping and cue reweighting share a similar time-course (significant correlation between the amount of remapping and reweighting across sessions; Figure 3A, r = 0.81, P = 0.028), the overall amount of cue remapping exhibited by each subject was independent of the amount of cue reweighting (Figure 3B, r = 0.03, P = 0.90).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The overall amount of cue remapping exhibited by each subject was independent of the amount of cue reweighting.
source: Although cue remapping and cue reweighting share a similar time-course (significant correlation between the amount of remapping and reweighting across sessions; Figure 3A, r = 0.81, P = 0.028), the overall amount of cue remapping exhibited by each subject was independent of the amount of cue reweighting (Figure 3B, r = 0.03, P = 0.90).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Inter-subject variability in adaptive processes was not attributable to differences in the effectiveness of earplugs used.
source: This inter-subject variability was not attributable to differences in the effectiveness of earplugs used (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cue remapping and cue reweighting are affected by the frequency composition of the stimulus in different ways.
source: Instead, we found that these two adaptive processes are affected by the frequency composition of the stimulus in different ways (Figure 3C, interaction between sound frequency and adaptation type, p = 0.005, permutation test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cue reweighting was greater for frequencies where spectral cues are most prominent in humans (≥4 kHz).
source: As expected, cue reweighting was greater for frequencies where spectral cues are most prominent in humans (≥4 kHz, Figure 3C, p<0.05, post-hoc test; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) (Blauert, 1997; Hofman and Van Opstal, 2002), whereas equal amounts of cue remapping were observed for tones above and below 4 kHz (Figure 3C, p>0.05, post-hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and citations to prior research.

claim: Equal amounts of cue remapping were observed for tones above and below 4 kHz.
source: As expected, cue reweighting was greater for frequencies where spectral cues are most prominent in humans (≥4 kHz, Figure 3C, p<0.05, post-hoc test; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) (Blauert, 1997; Hofman and Van Opstal, 2002), whereas equal amounts of cue remapping were observed for tones above and below 4 kHz (Figure 3C, p>0.05, post-hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no correlation between the degree of cue reweighting and remapping in cortical neurons recorded from ferrets raised with one ear plugged.
source: In common with our human behavioral data, we found no correlation between the degree of cue reweighting and remapping in cortical neurons recorded from ferrets raised with one ear plugged (Figure 3E, r = 0.08, p = 0.073).
evidence: This claim is supported by neurophysiological data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The type of plasticity observed in ferret cortical neurons depended on the frequency preference of the neurons.
source: The type of plasticity observed also depended on the frequency preference of the neurons (Figure 3F, interaction between unit characteristic frequency and adaptation process, p = 0.012, permutation test).
evidence: This claim is supported by neurophysiological data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Greater cue reweighting was found in ferret neurons tuned to frequencies where spectral cues are most prominent in ferrets (>8 kHz).
source: Greater cue reweighting was found in neurons tuned to frequencies where spectral cues are most prominent in ferrets (>8 kHz, Figure 3F, p<0.05, post-hoc test; frequency tuning bandwidth at 10 dB above threshold (µ ± SD) = 0.97 ± 0.51 octaves) (Carlile and King, 1994; Keating et al., 2013), whereas equal amounts of cue remapping occurred in neurons tuned to low and high frequencies (Figure 3F, p>0.05, post-hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by neurophysiological data, statistical analysis, and citations to prior research.

claim: Equal amounts of cue remapping occurred in ferret neurons tuned to low and high frequencies.
source: Greater cue reweighting was found in neurons tuned to frequencies where spectral cues are most prominent in ferrets (>8 kHz, Figure 3F, p<0.05, post-hoc test; frequency tuning bandwidth at 10 dB above threshold (µ ± SD) = 0.97 ± 0.51 octaves) (Carlile and King, 1994; Keating et al., 2013), whereas equal amounts of cue remapping occurred in neurons tuned to low and high frequencies (Figure 3F, p>0.05, post-hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by neurophysiological data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Different neurons can exhibit cue remapping and reweighting in a relatively independent manner.
source: Thus, different neurons can exhibit cue remapping and reweighting in a relatively independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the neurophysiological findings showing independence between the two processes.

claim: Adult humans can adapt to asymmetric hearing loss by both learning to rely more on unchanged spectral localization cues and by remapping altered binaural cues onto appropriate spatial locations.
source: We have shown that adult humans can adapt to asymmetric hearing loss by both learning to rely more on the unchanged spectral localization cues available and by remapping the altered binaural cues onto appropriate spatial locations.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings of the study.

claim: Both adaptive processes (cue remapping and reweighting) occur in response to monaural deprivation during development.
source: Recent work has shown that both adaptive processes occur in response to monaural deprivation during development (Keating et al., 2013; 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The flexibility to use both adaptive processes is likely to be a general feature of neural processing that also occurs in adulthood.
source: Our results suggest that this flexibility is likely to be a general feature of neural processing that also occurs in adulthood.
evidence: This is inferred from the current study's findings in adult humans.

claim: Both forms of adaptation (cue remapping and reweighting) emerge together.
source: Moreover, we show that these two forms of adaptation emerge together and that remapping of binaural spatial cues occurs at low as well as high frequencies, indicating plasticity in the processing of both ITDs and ILDs.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing similar time-courses for both processes.

claim: Remapping of binaural spatial cues occurs at low as well as high frequencies, indicating plasticity in the processing of both ITDs and ILDs.
source: Moreover, we show that these two forms of adaptation emerge together and that remapping of binaural spatial cues occurs at low as well as high frequencies, indicating plasticity in the processing of both ITDs and ILDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of remapping at different frequencies.

claim: Much shorter periods of training are sufficient to induce adaptation to an episodic hearing loss compared to prolonged earplug wearing.
source: Although adaptive changes in sound localization have previously been observed when human subjects wear an earplug for prolonged periods of everyday life (Kumpik et al., 2010), we found here that much shorter periods of training are sufficient to induce adaptation to an episodic hearing loss.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's findings and prior research.

claim: Previous work showed that cue remapping did not occur when subjects wore an earplug most of the time for several days with relatively little training.
source: In contrast, previous work has shown that cue remapping did not occur when subjects wore an earplug most of the time for several days, and were therefore able to interact with their natural environments under these hearing conditions, but received relatively little training (Kumpik et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The nature of adaptation may depend on the behavioral or environmental context in which it occurs.
source: This suggests that the nature of adaptation may depend on the behavioral or environmental context in which it occurs.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between different training paradigms and their outcomes.

claim: It should be possible to devise training protocols that would help subjects to adapt to altered auditory inputs in ways that do not ordinarily occur, or occur more slowly, during the course of everyday life.
source: Consequently, it should be possible to devise training protocols that would help subjects to adapt to altered auditory inputs in ways that do not ordinarily occur, or occur more slowly, during the course of everyday life.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings about training effects.

claim: The spatial cues involved in cue remapping and reweighting differ in their frequency dependence.
source: This is at least in part because the spatial cues involved differ in their frequency dependence.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed frequency-dependent differences in the two adaptive processes.

claim: Equal amounts of binaural cue remapping occurred at different frequencies, spanning the range where both ITDs and ILDs are available.
source: Whereas equal amounts of binaural cue remapping occurred at different frequencies, spanning the range where both ITDs and ILDs are available, reweighting of spectral cues was restricted to those frequencies where these cues are most prominent.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data on frequency-dependent adaptation.

claim: Reweighting of spectral cues was restricted to those frequencies where these cues are most prominent.
source: Whereas equal amounts of binaural cue remapping occurred at different frequencies, spanning the range where both ITDs and ILDs are available, reweighting of spectral cues was restricted to those frequencies where these cues are most prominent.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data on frequency-dependent adaptation.

claim: The neural substrates for cue remapping and reweighting are at least partially distinct.
source: This suggests that the neural substrates for cue remapping and reweighting are at least partially distinct, with separate populations of cortical neurons displaying different types of spatial plasticity depending on their frequency preferences and sensitivity to different spatial cues.
evidence: This is inferred from the neurophysiological findings showing different neurons exhibit different types of plasticity.

claim: Separate populations of cortical neurons display different types of spatial plasticity depending on their frequency preferences and sensitivity to different spatial cues.
source: This suggests that the neural substrates for cue remapping and reweighting are at least partially distinct, with separate populations of cortical neurons displaying different types of spatial plasticity depending on their frequency preferences and sensitivity to different spatial cues.
evidence: This is inferred from the neurophysiological data showing frequency-dependent differences in plasticity.

claim: Experience-dependent plasticity in the processing of binaural cues has been observed at multiple levels of the auditory pathway.
source: Although experience-dependent plasticity in the processing of binaural cues has been observed at multiple levels of the auditory pathway (Keating et al., 2015; Popescu and Polley, 2010; Seidl and Grothe, 2005), the changes induced by unilateral hearing loss during development are more extensive in the cortex than in the midbrain (Popescu and Polley, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The changes induced by unilateral hearing loss during development are more extensive in the cortex than in the midbrain.
source: Although experience-dependent plasticity in the processing of binaural cues has been observed at multiple levels of the auditory pathway (Keating et al., 2015; Popescu and Polley, 2010; Seidl and Grothe, 2005), the changes induced by unilateral hearing loss during development are more extensive in the cortex than in the midbrain (Popescu and Polley, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Reweighting of spectral cues is likely to reflect a change in the way they are integrated with other cues, which is thought to occur in the inferior colliculus.
source: However, reweighting of these cues is likely to reflect a change in the way they are integrated with other cues, which is thought to occur in the inferior colliculus (Chase and Young, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference and a citation to prior research.

claim: Adaptive changes in sound localization behavior in monaurally deprived adult ferrets rely on descending projections from the cortex to the inferior colliculus.
source: This is consistent with the finding that adaptive changes in sound localization behavior in monaurally deprived adult ferrets rely on descending projections from the cortex to the inferior colliculus (Bajo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Adaptive plasticity likely emerges via dynamic interactions between different stages of processing.
source: It is likely therefore that adaptive plasticity emerges via dynamic interactions between different stages of processing (Keating and King, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on inference and a citation.

claim: Ferrets had one ear occluded for ~80% of the time over the course of several months of development.
source: Whereas ferrets had one ear occluded for ~80% of the time over the course of several months of development (Keating et al., 2013; 2015), adult human subjects wore an earplug for only ~7 hr in total (1 hr every 1–3 days).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in prior ferret studies.

claim: Adult human subjects wore an earplug for only ~7 hr in total (1 hr every 1–3 days).
source: Whereas ferrets had one ear occluded for ~80% of the time over the course of several months of development (Keating et al., 2013; 2015), adult human subjects wore an earplug for only ~7 hr in total (1 hr every 1–3 days).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the current study.

claim: It is not known whether comparable physiological changes to those observed in ferrets are responsible for the rapid shifts in localization strategy in adult human listeners.
source: It is not known whether comparable physiological changes to those observed in the ferrets are responsible for the rapid shifts in localization strategy in adult human listeners following these brief periods of acute hearing loss.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in the current understanding.

claim: The close similarity in the results obtained in humans and ferrets has important implications for the generality of the findings.
source: Nevertheless, the close similarity in the results obtained in each species has important implications for the generality of our findings.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of results across species.

claim: The results emphasize the flexibility of neural systems when changes in sensory input affect ethologically important aspects of sensory processing.
source: Our results emphasize the flexibility of neural systems when changes in sensory input affect ethologically important aspects of sensory processing, such as sound localization.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The results reveal individual differences in the adaptive strategy adopted.
source: They also reveal individual differences in the adaptive strategy adopted (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The results highlight the importance of training in promoting multiple adaptive processes.
source: Our results also highlight the importance of training in promoting multiple adaptive processes, and this is likely to be relevant to other aspects of sensory processing (Feldman and Brecht, 2005; Keating and King, 2015; Sengpiel, 2014), particularly in situations where changes in sensory input affect some cues but not others.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: 11 audiologically normal human subjects (2 male, 9 female; aged 18–30) took part in the behavioral study.
source: 11 audiologically normal human subjects (2 male, 9 female; aged 18–30) took part in the behavioral study.
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: Neurophysiological data were obtained from 13 ferrets (6 male, 7 female), seven of which were reared with an intermittent unilateral hearing loss.
source: Neurophysiological data were obtained from 13 ferrets (6 male, 7 female), seven of which were reared with an intermittent unilateral hearing loss, the details of which have been described previously (Keating et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the animal subjects used in the study.

claim: Earplugs were first introduced to the left ear of ferrets between postnatal day 25 and 29, shortly after the age of hearing onset in these animals.
source: Briefly, earplugs were first introduced to the left ear of ferrets between postnatal day 25 and 29, shortly after the age of hearing onset in these animals.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for ferrets.

claim: From postnatal day 25-29 onwards, ferret earplugs were worn ~80% of the time within any 15-day period, with normal hearing experienced otherwise.
source: From then on, an earplug was worn ~80% of the time within any 15-day period, with normal hearing experienced otherwise.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for ferrets.

claim: Earplugs attenuated (low-pass filter, attenuation of 20–40 dB in humans, and 15–45 dB in ferrets) and delayed (150 µs in humans and 110 µs in ferrets) acoustical input.
source: For both human and animal subjects, hearing loss was induced by inserting an earplug into one ear (EAR Classic), which attenuated (low-pass filter, attenuation of 20–40 dB in humans, and 15–45 dB in ferrets) and delayed (150 µs in humans and 110 µs in ferrets) acoustical input (Keating et al., 2013; Kumpik et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the effect of the earplugs used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: Stimuli were presented using a circular array (1 m radius) of 12 loudspeakers placed at approximately head height, with loudspeakers positioned at 30° intervals.
source: Stimuli were presented to subjects using a circular array (1 m radius) of 12 loudspeakers (Audax TW025M0) placed at approximately head height, with loudspeakers positioned at 30° intervals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus, illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All stimuli were 100 ms in duration (including 10 ms cosine ramps), generated with a sampling rate of 97.6 kHz, and presented at 49–77 dB SPL in increments of 7 dB.
source: All stimuli were 100 ms in duration (including 10 ms cosine ramps), generated with a sampling rate of 97.6 kHz, and presented at 49–77 dB SPL in increments of 7 dB.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the study.

claim: Subjects completed 7 training sessions over ~3 weeks, with no more than 2 days between each session.
source: Subjects completed 7 training sessions over ~3 weeks, with no more than 2 days between each session.
evidence: This describes the training protocol used in the study.

claim: Each training session comprised ~800 trials and lasted ~45 min, with short breaks provided every ~15 min.
source: Each session comprised ~800 trials and lasted ~45 min, with short breaks provided every ~15 min.
evidence: This describes the training protocol used in the study.

claim: Recent work has shown that head-movements may enhance adaptation to changes in auditory spatial cues.
source: Recent work has shown that head-movements may enhance adaptation to changes in auditory spatial cues (Carlile et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Bilateral extracellular recordings were made under medetomidine/ketamine anaesthesia from primary auditory cortex units (n = 505) in response to virtual acoustic space stimuli.
source: Bilateral extracellular recordings were made under medetomidine/ketamine anaesthesia from primary auditory cortex units (n = 505) in response to virtual acoustic space stimuli generated from acoustical measurements in each animal.
evidence: This describes the neurophysiological recording methods.

claim: Virtual acoustic space stimuli recreated the acoustical conditions associated with either normal hearing or an earplug in the left ear.
source: These stimuli recreated the acoustical conditions associated with either normal hearing or an earplug in the left ear and were used to manipulate individual spatial cues independently of one another.
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in neurophysiological recordings.

claim: Cue weights were determined by calculating the mutual information between neuronal responses and individual spatial cues.
source: Cue weights were determined by calculating the mutual information between neuronal responses and individual spatial cues.
evidence: This describes the analysis method used for neurophysiological data.

claim: A weighting index was used to calculate the weight given by each neuron to spectral cues provided by the right ear relative to all other available cues.
source: A weighting index was then used to calculate the weight given by each neuron to spectral cues provided by the right ear (i.e. contralateral to the developmentally-occluded ear) relative to all other available cues.
evidence: This describes the analysis method used for neurophysiological data.

claim: The mapping between binaural spatial cues and neurophysiological responses was measured by determining the best ILD for each unit.
source: The mapping between binaural spatial cues and neurophysiological responses was measured by determining the best ILD for each unit, which represented the ILD corresponding to the peak of the binaural interaction function (see Keating et al., 2015 for more details).
evidence: This describes the analysis method used for neurophysiological data, with reference to prior work.

claim: When one ear is plugged, sounds presented on one side of the head will be louder and arrive earlier at the ipsilateral ear, producing interaural time and level differences.
source: When one of these sounds is presented on one side of the head, it will be louder and arrive earlier at the ipsilateral ear (blue), producing interaural time and level differences, which are respectively the primary cues to sound location at low and high frequencies.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1A and represents established knowledge about binaural cues.

claim: Interaural time and level differences are respectively the primary cues to sound location at low and high frequencies.
source: When one of these sounds is presented on one side of the head, it will be louder and arrive earlier at the ipsilateral ear (blue), producing interaural time and level differences, which are respectively the primary cues to sound location at low and high frequencies.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1A and represents established knowledge about binaural cues.

claim: The spectrum of a sound at the tympanic membrane differs from that of the original sound and varies with location due to acoustic filtering by the head and ears.
source: Because of acoustic filtering by the head and ears, the spectrum of a sound at the tympanic membrane (post-filtering, color) differs from that of the original sound (pre-filtering, black) and varies with location (amplitude in dB is plotted as a function of frequency; color indicates different locations).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1B and represents established knowledge about spectral cues.

claim: Spectral cues make it possible to localize sounds using a single ear, but only for sounds that have relatively flat spectra and are sufficiently broadband.
source: These spectral cues make it possible to localize sounds using a single ear, but only for sounds that have relatively flat spectra (solid lines) and are sufficiently broadband (shape of spectra in narrow frequency bands varies little with location – see shaded gray region).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1B and represents established knowledge about spectral cues.

claim: When spectral features are artificially added to the pre-filtered sound source, these added features can be misattributed to the filtering effects of the head and ears, producing sound localization errors.
source: When spectral features are artificially added to the pre-filtered sound source (dotted lines), these added features can be misattributed to the filtering effects of the head and ears. This produces sound localization errors (e.g. dotted green spectrum is more easily confused with solid turquoise spectrum because of additional peak at high frequencies).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1B and explains the rationale for using random-spectrum stimuli.

claim: The extent of localization errors with random-spectrum stimuli allows inference of subjects' reliance on spectral cues.
source: The extent of these errors allows us to infer subjects' reliance on spectral cues.
evidence: This explains the methodological approach illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Sound localization performance declined as spectral randomization increased at high frequencies.
source: This indicates that some of our random-spectrum stimuli were more difficult to localize than others, with performance declining as spectral randomization increased at high frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Increasing amounts of spectral randomization progressively degrade the usefulness of spectral cues, which are most prominent at high frequencies.
source: It also supports the view that increasing amounts of spectral randomization progressively degrade the usefulness of spectral cues, which are most prominent at high frequencies.
evidence: This is inferred from data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and represents the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: The amount of spectral randomization was smaller for correctly localized stimuli compared to mislocalized stimuli, but only at higher frequencies.
source: Relative to mislocalized stimuli, we found that the amount of spectral randomization was smaller for correctly localized stimuli, but only at higher frequencies (D, indicated by asterisk; significant interaction between frequency and correctness of response, P < 0.001, ANOVA; P < 0.05, post hoc test).
evidence: This is supported by data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The spectra of correctly-localized sounds tended to be relatively flat at high frequencies.
source: In other words, the spectra of correctly-localized sounds tended to be relatively flat at high frequencies.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No differences in sound level were observed between stimuli on correct and incorrect trials.
source: No differences in sound level were observed between stimuli on correct and incorrect trials (E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Adaptation occurs for both flat- and random-spectrum stimuli when measured by changes in error magnitude.
source: Adaptation occurs for both flat- and random-spectrum stimuli (Δ error values are significantly <0; p<0.01, bootstrap test), but the extent of adaptation is greater for flat-spectrum stimuli (p<0.01, bootstrap test on the within-subject differences in Δ error).
evidence: This is supported by data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The extent of adaptation is greater for flat-spectrum stimuli than random-spectrum stimuli when measured by changes in error magnitude.
source: Adaptation occurs for both flat- and random-spectrum stimuli (Δ error values are significantly <0; p<0.01, bootstrap test), but the extent of adaptation is greater for flat-spectrum stimuli (p<0.01, bootstrap test on the within-subject differences in Δ error).
evidence: This is supported by data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: No changes in response bias were observed for either flat- or random-spectrum stimuli.
source: No changes in bias were observed for either stimulus type (Δ bias values do not deviate significantly from 0;p>0.05, bootstrap test).
evidence: This is supported by data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H.

claim: A significant correlation was observed between earplug attenuation (Δ threshold) and the initial drop in sound localization performance.
source: A significant correlation (p<0.05) was observed between Δ threshold and the initial drop in sound localization performance when an earplug was worn during the first training session (Δ performance; change in% correct relative to normal hearing conditions averaged across all stimulus types).
evidence: This is supported by data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Initial sound localization deficits were more extensive when the earplug produced greater attenuation.
source: In other words, initial sound localization deficits were more extensive when the earplug produced greater attenuation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No obvious relationship was observed between earplug attenuation (Δ threshold) and the degree of remapping or reweighting observed in individual subjects.
source: No obvious relationship was observed between Δ threshold and the degree of remapping (C) or reweighting (D) observed in individual subjects (dots).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Distinct spectral features emerged when averaging random-spectrum stimuli was restricted to trials on which subjects responded to a particular location.
source: Although the mean spectrum of random-spectrum stimuli was close to zero when averaged across all trials (black), distinct spectral features emerged when averaging was restricted to trials on which subjects responded to a particular location (gray/color). This provides insight into which spectral features influence sound localization behavior.
evidence: This is supported by data and analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Cue reweighting values significantly greater than chance were observed at high frequencies.
source: Dotted line shows the upper 95% confidence interval for cue reweighting values that would be expected under the null hypothesis that cue reweighting did not occur. Values above this line (red symbols) indicate cue reweighting values that are significantly greater than chance.
evidence: This is supported by data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.
